analysis.one_liner: Expands the overtime-pay exemption to cover far more computer and IT workers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to exempt more IT workers from overtime pay was referred to the Senate labor committee in October 2011 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Computer Professionals Update Act would rewrite the part of federal wage law that lets employers skip paying time-and-a-half overtime to certain computer workers. It would stretch that exemption to cover any worker in a computer or information technology occupation — including network, database, security, and website work — and add job titles like designer, developer, and administrator. It would also let employers claim the exemption by paying a salary at whatever level existing Labor Department rules set, instead of the current hourly pay floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Software companies, IT departments, and tech staffing and outsourcing firms gain the most: they could classify a wider range of computer employees — including salaried workers paid under the current hourly threshold — as exempt, and stop paying time-and-a-half for hours over 40.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tech employers and IT staffing firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill broadens the Fair Labor Standards Act overtime exemption to reach any employee working in a computer or information technology occupation, including work on networks, databases, security, and websites, and adds designer, developer, and administrator to the covered titles.

It extends the exemption to workers paid at least $27.63 an hour, as under current law, or on a salary basis at a salary level set by the Department of Labor's existing regulations — opening a path for salaried workers below the hourly floor to be classified as exempt.
Covered IT employees would be treated as exempt professionals under the wage law's professional exemption, removing overtime-pay obligations for their employers.

analysis.who_pays: IT employees in the newly covered occupations would lose the right to overtime pay — time-and-a-half for hours worked beyond 40 — for the same work they do today. The bill's broad language, which sweeps in network administration, security, and website work, could also reach workers who are not highly paid software engineers.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets an employer avoid overtime pay by putting a computer employee on a salary at whatever level the Labor Department's existing rules set, rather than the current $27.63-an-hour pay floor — meaning moderately paid salaried IT staff could lose overtime protections.

The exemption would cover a broad list of occupations beyond programming, including network, database, security, and website work, which could sweep in lower-skilled or lower-paid technical support jobs that current law treats as overtime-eligible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a labor-cost saving to tech employers but takes pay from a slice of the workforce: affected IT employees would work the same hours for less when weeks run past 40 hours. The hourly floor of $27.63 protects well-paid contractors, but the new salary-basis route and the wide list of covered occupations leave room for moderate earners to be classified out of overtime. On balance, the costs fall on workers and the gains accrue to employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee in October 2011, and that committee never acted on it; the Congress ended in January 2013 without the bill ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Hagan introduced the bill on October 20, 2011, joined by Senators Isakson, Enzi, and Bennet, with a cosponsor list of eight senators — seven Republicans and one Democrat.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in committee with no markup, no floor vote, and no House consideration for the rest of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: IT workers are better off because the bill died: they kept the overtime rights and pay floors they had under the narrower existing exemption, and tech employers never gained the wider ability to classify employees as overtime-exempt.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: IT workers who kept overtime rights

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backing was genuinely bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor joined by seven Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — and its death was a committee inaction rather than a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: The bill would let these employers skip time-and-a-half pay for a much wider set of computer employees, including salaried workers below the current hourly threshold. The saving comes directly out of overtime pay that workers would otherwise receive.
Firms whose business model depends on billing IT labor would gain flexibility to classify billed employees as exempt and avoid overtime costs on long workweeks.

Employees in the newly covered occupations would lose overtime pay for hours over 40 unless individually negotiated. Low and moderate earners in network, security, or website-support roles had the most at risk under the broad wording.
